title: Benefits of Genetic Technologies: Agriculture, Medicine and Industry
subtitle: Bacteria making insulin and an edited human embryo both used genetic technology to promise a health benefit, yet one is accepted worldwide and the other was condemned. So which benefits of genetic technology actually hold up, and how can you tell?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: stating that a benefit must be better than an alternative, shown by evidence and received by someone, and testing a claim with "Better than what? Shown how? Who gets it?"; explaining why the 2018 embryo edit fails all three (an existing method already protected the embryos, and HIV can be prevented in other ways later in life; the edits were untested and did not copy the natural protective variant; the children carried the risk without consent); evaluating virus-resistant papaya (no ordinary variety resisted the virus; harvests climbed back after 1998, to about three quarters of the earlier level by 2001; growers gained); evaluating recombinant insulin (it controls blood sugar about as well as purified pig insulin for most patients, so its clear benefit is a reliable, scalable supply; access depends on price); explaining why recombinant growth hormone's benefit is larger (the old pituitary source was scarce and some batches spread a fatal brain disease); evaluating microbe-made chymosin (the same enzyme without depending on calves); explaining why agriculture is the most contested domain (organisms are released, so pests evolve and crop genetic diversity can narrow; Bt cotton's benefit holds while refuges keep resistance rare); ranking benefits by irreplaceability, evidence and reach rather than by how advanced the technology is (growth hormone and the papaya far better than what came before, with clear evidence; insulin and chymosin clear on supply; growth hormone's and insulin's reach depend on cost); applying this to an unseen assess item and an unseen evaluate item.

voiceover.text: In 1982, human insulin made by bacteria was approved, and it's now used around the world. In 2018, a researcher edited a gene in human embryos, hoping twin girls would resist HIV. Scientists everywhere condemned it, and he was sent to prison. Both used genetic technology, and both promised a health benefit. So that label alone can't tell you which one to trust. Which benefits actually hold up, and how can you tell?

A benefit is never just good in general. It's better than something, shown by evidence, for someone. So ask three questions. Better than what? Shown how? Who gets it? Try them on the embryo edit. The father had HIV, but washing his sperm before IVF already protects an embryo, and HIV can be prevented in other ways later in life. The edits didn't copy the natural protective version of the gene, and their effects were untested. And the twins carried all the risk, with no say. It fails all three.

Start on the farm, where benefits include harvests, pest resistance and nutrition. In the nineteen-nineties, a virus was killing papaya trees across Hawaii's main growing district, and no ordinary variety resisted it. Scientists gave papaya a copy of one of the virus's genes. The plant's cells use it to recognise the virus's genetic material and destroy it. Better than what? Trees that were dying. Shown how? The district's harvest had roughly halved, and after growers got the seed in 1998, harvests climbed back. Who gets it? The growers. That benefit holds up strongly.

Now medicine. Bacteria make human insulin. Better than what? Insulin from pig and cattle pancreases. Pig insulin differs from ours by one amino acid, and cattle insulin by three. You'd expect the human version to work much better. But when trials compared them, purified pig insulin controlled blood sugar about as well for most patients. So the benefit that holds up isn't a better medicine. It's the supply. Insulin no longer depends on pancreases from abattoirs, and fermenters make a consistent product at scale. Who gets it? That depends on price. Many people with diabetes worldwide still can't reliably get it.

Now compare growth hormone, given to children whose bodies don't make enough. Until 1985, it came from the pituitary glands of people who had died. Supply was scarce, and some batches carried a fatal brain disease. That year it was withdrawn, and hormone made by bacteria replaced it. The old source was scarce and dangerous, so the benefit is far bigger. Better than what sets how much a benefit is worth.

Industry follows the same logic. Once a microbe makes a useful protein, it can make it at factory scale. Take chymosin, the enzyme that curdles milk for cheese. It used to come from calves' stomachs. Better than what? Microbes now make the same enzyme, so the cheese turns out the same, and supply doesn't depend on calves. Shown how? Since about 1990, it's been used for much of the world's cheese. Who gets it? Cheesemakers, with a steady supply at lower cost.

In medicine and industry, the engineered microbes usually stay sealed in tanks, and only the purified product leaves. On a farm, the modified organism is released. It grows among wild species, its pests can evolve resistance, and if one variety is planted everywhere, the crop's genetic diversity narrows. That's why Bt cotton's benefit, far fewer sprays than ordinary cotton, holds up only while refuges keep resistance rare. A gain in harvest isn't a gain in biodiversity.

So which benefits hold up best? They're strongest where the technology did something the old method couldn't do safely, the evidence measures the real outcome, and the product reaches the people who need it. Growth hormone and the papaya were far better than what came before, with clear evidence. Insulin and chymosin win clearly on supply, though insulin's reach depends on price. Other farm crops can bring big benefits, but the verdict depends on how they're managed, and who gains. So a benefit isn't measured by how advanced the technology is.
Here's the test in three questions. Better than what? Shown how? Who gets it? And one reminder for the farm: a gain in harvest isn't a gain in biodiversity.

Two exam questions. First. A company makes laundry enzymes using genetically modified microbes. The enzymes remove stains at twenty degrees, where older detergents needed forty to sixty. Most of the energy a washing machine uses goes into heating the water. The company claims its enzymes cut household energy use. Assess this claim. Pause here to answer.

The claim holds only partly. Compared with a hot wash, a twenty degree wash saves most of the energy, because heating the water uses the most. But the enzyme only makes a cold wash possible. The saving happens only if people choose cold washes, so you'd want measured energy use in real homes. Saying the enzyme saves energy by itself is the classic mistake.

Second. The first hepatitis B vaccine, from 1981, used a virus protein purified from the blood plasma of people who carried the virus. From 1986, yeast carrying the gene for the same protein made it in fermenters. Both vaccines protected well. Evaluate the benefit of the yeast-made vaccine compared with the plasma vaccine. Pause here to answer.

Protection wasn't the gain, because both protected well. The gain was supply. It no longer depended on plasma from infected donors, it could be made consistently at large scale, and it eased fears of infection from blood products. That helped make vaccinating every baby practical, as Australia does. So the benefit is large, and it rests on supply and safety. Saying it protects better is the classic mistake.

So to evaluate a benefit, name the domain and the exact benefit. Then ask: better than what, shown how, and who gets it? Weigh it against the trade-offs, especially biodiversity on farms, and finish with a verdict. Next, practice questions that weigh benefits against biodiversity and ethics.
